title: Machine Learning Foundations
subtitle: The 20% of ML that explains 80% of modern AI

slides.title: Why this module exists
bullets: Transformers, agents and RAG are ML wearing a bigger coat
Three ideas carry the whole track: a loss, a gradient, a validation split
If you skip this, later modules feel like magic instead of engineering
Target: explain bias/variance and leakage to a colleague, unaided
slides.notes: Set expectations: this module is the vocabulary for everything downstream.

slides.title: Classical programming vs. machine learning
bullets: Classical: rules + data -> answers
ML: data + answers -> rules (a model)
A model is f_theta(x) -> y_hat plus a procedure to choose theta
'Training' = minimise a loss over data
Don't use ML when the rule is known, labels are unobtainable, or errors are unacceptable
slides.notes: The 'when not to use ML' list is the most useful slide for business stakeholders.

slides.title: The three-and-a-half paradigms
slides.notes: Self-supervised is the half - and the reason LLMs scaled. Next-token prediction is supervised learning with free labels.

slides.title: Empirical risk minimisation
bullets: J(theta) = (1/n) * sum L(f(x_i), y_i)  +  lambda * R(theta)
Left term: fit the data. Right term: don't get carried away
We minimise empirical risk but we care about TRUE risk
The entire field of generalization lives in that gap
slides.notes: Write the equation on a whiteboard. Everything else is commentary.

slides.title: Losses you must recognise on sight
rows: this is the LLM training loss
slides.notes: Highlight row 4 - it links directly to Module 04.

slides.title: Model families that still matter
bullets: Linear / logistic regression - interpretable, fast, and literally one neuron
k-NN - no training; this IS vector search (Module 08)
Decision trees -> Random Forest (cuts variance) -> Gradient boosting (cuts bias)
Gradient-boosted trees still beat deep nets on medium tabular data
Know also: SVM, Naive Bayes, PCA, k-Means
slides.notes: Push back on 'use deep learning for everything'. Tabular is boosting's home turf.

slides.title: Features win projects; models rarely do
bullets: Scale numerics for distance- and gradient-based models; trees don't care
Categoricals: one-hot -> target encoding (inside CV folds!) -> embeddings
Never build a feature from information that post-dates the prediction
Missingness is a signal - add an is_missing flag
Model choice is ~10% of the outcome
slides.notes: Ask the room for their worst feature-engineering war story.

slides.title: Data leakage
slides.quote: Any information in training that will not exist at prediction time.
bullets: Symptom: suspiciously high validation score, one dominant feature
Scaling/encoding before the split
Random splits on time series
IDs, timestamps, downstream artefacts, duplicate rows
slides.notes: This is the career-defining bug. Everyone ships it once.

slides.title: Pick the metric that matches the cost of being wrong
rows: of my alarms, how many were real?
of the real cases, how many did I catch?
slides.notes: In a 99.9% negative dataset, 'always say no' scores 99.9% accuracy.

slides.title: Optimization: gradient descent
bullets: theta <- theta - eta * grad J(theta)
Learning rate eta is the single most important hyperparameter
Too small: crawls. Too large: diverges to NaN
Mini-batch (32-8192) won: GPU-friendly with useful noise
Adam -> AdamW (decoupled weight decay) trains modern LLMs
slides.notes: AdamW + linear warmup + cosine decay is the canonical LLM recipe.

slides.title: Reading a loss curve
rows: LR too low or broken labels
slides.notes: Smoke test: can the model overfit 10 examples to ~0 loss? If not, it's a bug, not a hyperparameter.

slides.title: Bias-variance
bullets: E[(y - f)^2] = Bias^2 + Variance + irreducible noise
High bias = underfit: wrong on train and test, consistently
High variance = overfit: great on train, swings with the sample
Irreducible noise = your label-quality ceiling
Double descent: past the interpolation threshold, test error can fall AGAIN
slides.notes: Double descent is the permission slip for trillion-parameter models.

slides.title: Validation strategy
bullets: Stratified k-fold is the classification default
Group k-fold when rows share an entity (patient, customer, session)
Time-series split: train on the past, validate on the future. Never shuffle time
Nested CV is the only unbiased way to report a tuned model's score
The test set is sacred - touch it once
slides.notes: Twenty peeks at the test set and your number is fiction.

slides.title: The test set is sacred
slides.quote: Benchmark contamination in LLMs is this exact bug, committed by an entire field at once.
bullets: Thousands of papers tuned against MMLU
MMLU stopped measuring what it claimed to
See Module 15 - AI Evaluation
slides.notes: Great transition slide if you are teaching the whole track.

slides.title: The workflow to internalise
bullets: Frame -> Baseline -> Split -> Explore -> Features
Model -> Tune -> Interpret -> Test once -> Ship & watch
Seniority shows in Frame, Explore, and Ship & watch
Everyone rushes to Model
Error analysis: read the 100 worst predictions, tag causes, fix the top one
slides.notes: Error analysis becomes 'failure taxonomy' in Module 15.

bullets: A notebook with: baseline, tuned model, leakage-free CV, calibration curve
One paragraph on when the model should NOT be trusted
